title: Ratio analysis (accounting)
examples: What is the difference between a liquidity ratio and a solvency ratio?
Can you show me how to calculate the current ratio?
If a ratio is high, does that always mean the business is doing well?

explain.say: Today we will learn about ratio analysis in accounting.
The current ratio measures short-term ability to pay debts.
Another important ratio is the debt-to-equity ratio for long-term health.
Interpretation means explaining what the calculated number suggests.
A real-life example is checking a friend's business finances.
A common mistake is assuming a single ratio tells the whole story.

items: Look at trends over several years

draw.text: Don't rely on one ratio only

faq.q: What exactly is the difference between liquidity and solvency?
faq.a: Liquidity ratios look at short-term debts, meaning immediate payments. Solvency ratios look at long-term ability to pay all debts.
asks: What is short-term vs long-term debt?
Do I use current ratio for short or long term?

faq.q: Why is the industry average important when interpreting ratios?
faq.a: Because what is good for one industry might be poor for another. You must compare it to similar businesses.
asks: Can I compare my ratio to my competitors?
Is there a benchmark for ratios?

faq.q: If my profit margin is very high, does that mean I am profitable?
faq.a: It suggests good profitability, but it does not tell you if you have enough cash to pay bills. Cash flow matters too.
asks: Is profit the same as cash?
What else should I check besides profit?

faq.q: Should I calculate ratios for every single account?
faq.a: No, you should focus on key ratios like current ratio and debt-to-equity. Too many ratios can confuse the analysis.
asks: Which ratios are the most important ones?
How many ratios should I calculate?

faq.q: What if my current ratio is below one?
faq.a: It suggests you might struggle to pay short-term debts with current assets. You need to improve cash management.
asks: What should I do if my ratio is low?

facts: The current ratio compares current assets to current liabilities.
The debt-to-equity ratio measures the proportion of debt to owner investment.
Interpretation requires comparing ratios to industry standards and past performance.
A ratio is a mathematical tool, not a final judgment on the business.

quiz.say: A business has current assets of eighty thousand and current liabilities of forty thousand. What is the current ratio?
quiz.why: The current ratio is calculated by dividing current assets by current liabilities, which is eighty divided by forty, giving two.

wrong.0: This incorrectly adds the two figures together instead of dividing.
wrong.1: This incorrectly reverses the order of division.
wrong.3: This incorrectly calculates the difference between the two figures.

quiz.say: If a company has a debt-to-equity ratio of 3, what does this suggest about its financing?

options.show: It relies heavily on borrowed money.
options.say: It relies heavily on borrowed money.

quiz.why: A ratio of three means that for every one unit of owner money, there are three units of debt, indicating high borrowing.

wrong.1: A high ratio suggests more risk from lenders' perspective.
wrong.2: This would result in a ratio of zero, not three.
wrong.3: This ratio measures structure, not immediate profitability.

quiz.say: When interpreting ratios, what is the most crucial step after calculating the number?

options.show: Assuming it must be above one.
options.say: Assuming it must be above one.

options.show: Rounding the number to the nearest whole number.
options.say: Rounding the number to the nearest whole number.

quiz.why: A number alone lacks context; comparing it to industry norms gives it meaning.

wrong.1: Some ratios can be acceptable below one depending on the sector.
wrong.2: You must interpret the first ratio before moving to the next one.
wrong.3: Losing decimal places can change the meaning of the ratio significantly.
